label: Space weather and satellite operations
description: The organizations that operate through space weather: a grid control room (a reliability coordinator and a transmission operator following a geomagnetic disturbance operating plan), a satellite operations center, and a GNSS timing and network operations team. The forecasts come from the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center: watches, warnings and alerts, the G, S and R scales, Kp, and X-ray and proton flux. Plans and standards: the grid operating plan and procedure (NERC EOP-010), transmission planning for geomagnetic disturbances (NERC TPL-007), satellite fault-protection and safe-mode procedures, and timing holdover limits. Variants: grid control room, satellite operations center, GNSS timing and network operations.

vocabulary.facility: the control room, the high-voltage transformers and substations, the ground station and satellites, and the timing sources at the network sites
vocabulary.public: customers without power or service, pilots and passengers on polar routes, farmers and surveyors who steer by GNSS, and satellite service subscribers
vocabulary.frontline: system operators, reliability coordinators, protection engineers, satellite flight controllers, network timing engineers and flight dispatchers
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the system operations control room (or the satellite operations center, or the network operations center)

roles.name: Reliability Coordinator Operator
roles.description: Owns the grid operating plan: passes forecast and current space weather information to the entities named in the plan and coordinates operating actions across the wide area.

roles.name: Transmission Operator System Operator
roles.description: Owns the operating procedure: actions at the predetermined conditions, the log, and the call to end them.

roles.name: Transmission Planner / Protection Engineer
roles.description: Owns the assessments, the GIC and transformer risk picture, relay misoperation checks and the post-event review.

roles.name: Generation Plant Operator
roles.description: Owns reactive support, unit protection settings and availability during the disturbance.

roles.name: Satellite Operations Engineer / Flight Director
roles.description: Owns safe-mode, attitude and drag management, anomaly response and notices to customers.

roles.name: Space Situational Awareness Analyst
roles.description: Owns tracking quality and conjunction risk when drag changes orbits.

roles.name: Network Timing Engineer
roles.team: Team E: Timing and Network Operations
roles.description: Owns holdover limits, failover to other time sources and the timing alarms.

roles.name: Airline Operations Control / Flight Dispatcher
roles.description: Owns reroutes away from polar and high-latitude paths, altitude choices and crew communications when HF fails.

roles.name: Farm or Survey Operations Lead
roles.description: Owns the call to stop or switch to non-GNSS guidance, and to resume when accuracy returns.

roles.name: Emergency Manager / State Grid Liaison
roles.description: Owns pre-positioning, shelters, communications and coordination of a long or wide outage.

roles.name: Public Information Officer
roles.description: Owns messages that state impacts and actions, not solar science, and keeps them consistent with partners.

a farm equipment forum thread about autosteer drifting
a space weather enthusiast's post on X/Twitter quoting the alert text
the local TV station's weather segment
an amateur radio net reporting HF conditions
a trade press story on satellite operators

sceneAnchors.public: on a dark rural road at night: a few people standing by parked cars with phones raised toward a faint green and red aurora, bare trees, clear sky, cold air
sceneAnchors.control: inside a transmission system control room: a wall of one-line diagrams and trend screens, operators at consoles with headsets, a binder labeled operating procedure on a desk, dim blue light

addedThreatFamilies.label: Severe geomagnetic storm
addedThreatFamilies.description: A coronal mass ejection is watched for one to three days in transit, then warned, then arrives; Kp climbs and the grid operating procedure must be applied before onset, with GNSS and HF effects following.

phaseArc.title: Flare and CME observed, watch issued
phaseArc.goal: Players see a geomagnetic storm watch with one to three days of lead time (up to 72 hours) and decide what to prepare and who to tell.
beats: A large flare is reported and a CME is modeled toward Earth
A geomagnetic storm watch lists the highest level predicted for each day
The reliability coordinator reviews the operating plan and the entities on its list

phaseArc.title: Warning as the CME approaches
phaseArc.goal: A warning narrows the time; the operating procedure's predetermined condition is near and the arrival time is uncertain by hours.
beats: A K-index warning is issued
The solar wind monitor shows the shock approaching with a stated arrival window
Operators ask whether to apply the procedure now or wait for the condition

phaseArc.title: Arrival and onset
phaseArc.goal: Kp crosses the condition; operating actions, GNSS errors and HF effects begin at once.
beats: A sudden commencement and a K-index alert follow
GIC readings rise at transformer neutrals
GNSS errors grow and an airline loses HF on polar routes

phaseArc.title: Peak, recovery and review
phaseArc.goal: Players decide when to end actions, keep GNSS-dependent work stopped, and review the record.
beats: Kp falls below the termination condition
Scintillation lingers and guidance accuracy stays poor for days at the highest levels
A review compares the log with the procedure and the messages sent

decisionPointExamples: apply the operating procedure at the warning and give up transfer capacity, or wait for Kp to cross the condition and risk acting after onset
end the procedure when Kp falls below the condition, or hold it through a second CME that is still inbound
tell the public to expect a long outage now on the watch, or wait for observed impacts and risk an unprepared community
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a geomagnetic storm watch or warning with a stated level, a solar wind speed step at the monitor upstream of Earth, a magnetometer disturbance at an observatory, a GIC reading at a transformer neutral
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a data feed from the upstream monitor that drops out at the worst time, relays that trip on harmonics, a stale forecast on a public display, GNSS time errors in the control room's own clocks
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center and the reliability coordinator
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Scale levels describe potential effects, and impacts are regional: they depend on geomagnetic latitude and ground conductivity. The G scale maps to Kp: G1 is Kp 5, G2 is 6, G3 is 7, G4 is 8 (and 9-), G5 is 9. CME arrival time is uncertain by hours; state the lead time the scenario assumes. Times are UTC in NOAA products. A watch is for elevated risk with uncertain timing, a warning for an event that is occurring, imminent or likely, and an alert says a threshold has been crossed. Do not give engineering advice about protection settings.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Solar radiation storm
addedThreatFamilies.description: A proton event raises particle flux at 10 MeV and above: polar HF is lost, satellites see single-event upsets, and aircraft on polar routes are rerouted.

phaseArc.title: Flare and rising proton flux
phaseArc.goal: Proton flux begins to rise after a flare; players see an alert threshold crossed.
beats: A flare is followed by a proton event alert
Flux crosses the S1 level and keeps rising
Dispatch asks about polar routes

phaseArc.title: Radiation level climbs
phaseArc.goal: The scale level rises to a level that affects satellites and polar flights.
beats: An alert reports the S3 level reached
A satellite reports a single-event upset
Polar HF communications become unreliable

phaseArc.title: Reroute and protect
phaseArc.goal: Players reroute flights, put satellites in a protective mode and tell customers.
beats: A flight is rerouted south of the polar region
A satellite is placed in safe mode ahead of the flux peak
A customer notice is drafted

phaseArc.title: Decay and return to service
phaseArc.goal: Flux decays over days; players decide when routes and satellites return to service.
beats: Flux falls below the S1 level
Satellites are brought out of safe mode in sequence
A review checks the crew and customer notices

decisionPointExamples: reroute the polar flight now at a fuel and schedule cost, or continue and rely on a backup communications path
put the satellite in safe mode before the flux peak and interrupt service, or keep service and accept upset risk
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a proton event alert with a stated level, a GOES proton flux series, a satellite upset count, a dispatcher's loss of HF contact
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: an alternate route closed by weather, a satellite telemetry gap, an airline with no secondary communications on the route
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center and the airline operations control center
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: S levels are tied to the flux of particles at or above 10 MeV (S1 is 10 particle flux units, each level ten times higher). Do not give radiation dose figures for crews. Aircraft decisions are the operator's; the exercise shows who decides and on what information.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Radio blackout from a flare
addedThreatFamilies.description: An X-ray flare blacks out HF radio on the sunlit side of Earth within minutes, with little warning, affecting aviation, maritime and amateur radio.

phaseArc.title: Active region
phaseArc.goal: An active region is flaring; no one has lost radio yet.
beats: An outlook notes the chance of strong flares
A moderate flare is reported
Dispatch asks what to expect

phaseArc.title: Flare and blackout
phaseArc.goal: A large flare blacks out HF on the sunlit side within minutes.
beats: A radio blackout alert reports the R level reached
Oceanic flights lose HF contact
A maritime operator reports no HF

phaseArc.title: Backup communications
phaseArc.goal: Players switch to other means and handle repeated flares.
beats: Satellite voice is used for position reports
A second flare follows an hour later
Controllers ask about separation

phaseArc.title: Recovery
phaseArc.goal: HF returns in tens of minutes to hours; players review the communications plan.
beats: HF contact returns on the lower bands first
A summary lists the flares of the day
A review finds a route without a backup

decisionPointExamples: hold flights at the oceanic boundary until contact returns, or continue on satellite voice and accept the workload
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a radio blackout alert with the R level and flare class, a GOES X-ray flux series, an HF contact loss report
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: no satellite voice on the aircraft, a ground station down, a second flare before the first has recovered
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center and air traffic services
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: R levels are tied to the peak GOES X-ray class: R1 is M1, R2 is M5, R3 is X1, R4 is X10, R5 is X20. The effect is on the sunlit side and lasts from minutes to hours; a flare gives no lead time.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Combined flare, radiation and CME event
addedThreatFamilies.description: One active region produces a flare, a radiation storm and then a CME: radio blackout, S-level radiation and a geomagnetic storm arrive in sequence and demands overlap.

phaseArc.title: Flare and blackout
phaseArc.goal: The flare comes first and with no warning.
beats: A radio blackout alert
A CME is seen in coronagraph images
Dispatch loses HF on a polar route

phaseArc.title: Radiation arrives
phaseArc.goal: A radiation storm begins while the CME is in transit.
beats: A proton event alert
A satellite upset
A storm watch is issued for the days ahead

phaseArc.title: Geomagnetic storm
phaseArc.goal: The CME arrives; the grid and GNSS effects stack on communications losses already in progress.
beats: A warning and then an alert for a high G level
GIC readings rise
GNSS error grows for farm and survey users

phaseArc.title: Days of recovery
phaseArc.goal: Several hazards decay on different clocks and players must sequence the return to service.
beats: HF returns, then flux falls, then Kp falls
GNSS accuracy stays poor for days
A joint review of the messages sent

decisionPointExamples: send one public message that covers radio, radiation and power now, or three separate messages and risk conflicting guidance
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a string of alerts with different codes in the order the hazards arrived, a coronagraph-based arrival forecast, reports from several sectors at once
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: staff stretched between hazards, a data feed gap during the peak, conflicting statements from partners
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center and state emergency management
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Keep the clocks separate: a flare's radio blackout lasts minutes to a few hours, a radiation storm hours to days, a geomagnetic storm hours to a day or more, and GNSS scintillation can last days after the peak. Messages across sectors should state the same severity and duration.

addedThreatFamilies.label: GNSS degradation and timing loss
addedThreatFamilies.description: Ionospheric disturbance degrades satellite navigation for hours to days: positions drift, fewer satellites are tracked, and timing receivers enter holdover until it expires.

phaseArc.title: Early errors
phaseArc.goal: Errors rise slightly; alarms are few and ambiguous.
beats: A timing engineer sees a few satellites lost
A farm customer reports guidance drifting
A storm warning is in effect

phaseArc.title: Holdover
phaseArc.goal: Receivers lose lock and enter holdover; the clock is running down.
beats: Timing alarms on several sites
Holdover remaining is below a few hours at the weakest site
The failover source is untested at one site

phaseArc.title: Failover or loss
phaseArc.goal: Players switch time sources before holdover expires or accept the consequences.
beats: A site passes its holdover limit
A network alarm storm hides the real fault
A dispatcher asks about GNSS approaches

phaseArc.title: Days of poor accuracy
phaseArc.goal: Scintillation lingers; users decide when to resume GNSS-guided work.
beats: Accuracy improves and worsens through the night
A farm cooperative asks when to resume planting
A review of time source diversity

decisionPointExamples: fail over to the alternate time source now and lose the primary's accuracy, or hold the GNSS source until holdover is nearly spent
resume GNSS-guided field work on a good reading, or wait for a stable day because errors return after dusk
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a timing alarm with satellites tracked, a horizontal error series, a receiver status report, a customer report of drift
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a failover source with its own GNSS dependency, a site with a short holdover oscillator, an alarm storm
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the network timing team and the GNSS equipment vendor
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Receiver classes differ: single-frequency, multi-frequency and a GNSS-disciplined oscillator with holdover stated in hours. State the class and the holdover. Errors are worst at night and near the equator and the poles. The exercise model is an illustration, not a prediction of real receiver performance.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Satellite anomaly or loss
addedThreatFamilies.description: Drag, charging or single-event upsets cause an anomaly: a safe-mode event, tracking uncertainty after an orbit change, or a lost satellite and an outage for customers.

phaseArc.title: Elevated environment
phaseArc.goal: The space environment is disturbed and the operator is on watch.
beats: A storm warning raises drag expectations
Telemetry shows a rise in memory errors
The flight director sets a heightened watch

phaseArc.title: Anomaly
phaseArc.goal: A satellite enters safe mode or its orbit changes faster than predicted.
beats: A safe-mode event on one satellite
Tracking data no longer match the predicted position
Customers report loss of service

phaseArc.title: Recovery and notices
phaseArc.goal: Players decide on commanded recovery, customer notices and conjunction screening.
beats: A recovery command sequence is reviewed
A conjunction warning cannot be assessed with stale tracking
A customer outage notice goes out

phaseArc.title: Lessons
phaseArc.goal: The operator reviews fault protection settings and notice timing.
beats: The satellite returns to service or is declared lost
A customer asks for a credit
A review of the safe-mode decision time

decisionPointExamples: command the satellite out of safe mode on a partial diagnosis, or wait and extend the customer outage
maneuver to avoid a conjunction with uncertain tracking, or hold and accept the risk
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a telemetry alarm, a tracking residual, a drag-driven altitude loss rate, a customer ticket
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: a ground station outage during the pass, stale tracking data, a command sequence that needs a second approval
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the space situational awareness provider and the satellite's customers
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Keep operating detail at the level of decisions and notices, not commanding or fault-protection settings. Effects are probabilistic: say what was observed, not that the storm caused it, until the operator concludes so.

addedThreatFamilies.label: Space weather information service degradation
addedThreatFamilies.description: The information needed to act fails or conflicts during the event: a data feed from a monitoring satellite drops out, a forecast office and a partner give different levels, or the notification chain does not reach an entity.

phaseArc.title: Normal watch
phaseArc.goal: Space weather information flows normally to the control room.
beats: A watch is in effect
The upstream solar wind data are current
A routine call between the coordinator and the operators

phaseArc.title: Loss of data
phaseArc.goal: A key data feed drops while conditions change.
beats: The solar wind monitor stops reporting
A Kp estimate lags the magnetometer
Staff debate what the missing data mean

phaseArc.title: Conflicting information
phaseArc.goal: Players decide on incomplete or conflicting levels from different sources.
beats: A partner message states a different level
A social media post quotes an old alert
An entity on the dissemination list did not receive the notice

phaseArc.title: Restore and review
phaseArc.goal: Data return with a gap; players compare their decisions with the record.
beats: The feed returns with a gap in the record
The log is checked against the plan's list of entities
A review of message consistency

decisionPointExamples: apply the procedure on the conservative reading of two conflicting sources, or wait for the official product
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a flat-lined data feed, a mismatch between two sources, a dissemination log with a missing recipient
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: an email subscription that failed silently, a stale display, a phone tree with an unreachable entity
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center and the reliability coordinator
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Missing data is not zero and not calm. The exercise should show how players tell a failed feed from a quiet Sun, and who must be told what.

noiseExamples: a routine request to move a maintenance outage date
an invoice for a software license renewal
a customer asking about a billing error
a vendor offering a webinar on transformer monitoring
a news story about a rocket launch schedule
pressureExamples: a reporter asking whether the lights will go out tonight
an aurora photo from a state far south of where it is usually seen, posted with a wrong claim of damage
a farm cooperative demanding to know when guidance will be accurate again
a commissioner asking why the operating procedure was applied when no outage followed
a satellite customer threatening to leave over an unannounced outage
a partner's message that states a higher storm level than the forecast office's
